rows: Inverters, SMPS, motor drives — specialized discipline
S-parameters, Smith chart, transmission line theory
Partially in 09; deep dive in semiconductor-manufacturing/
Full custom (not covered): bandgap references, PLLs, ADC architectures
Compare physical length to signal wavelength, edge rate, parasitic inductance/capacitance, and return path.
A board trace becomes a transmission line because of edge rate and geometry, not because the schematic changed.
Whether a problem is analog, digital, or mixed-signal
Identify whether information is represented by continuous voltage/current, logic thresholds, timing, or sampled values.
Digital failures often have analog causes: noise margins, ground bounce, jitter, and power integrity.
Locate poles/zeros, bandwidth, phase margin, sampling rate, aliasing risk, and load/source impedance.
The same math appears in analog filters, DSP, feedback amplifiers, and control loops.
Check gain-bandwidth, noise, input/output impedance, stability margin, slew rate, and supply headroom.
High DC gain is useless if the loop oscillates or saturates under real load.
Inspect impedance control, termination, return current, crosstalk, eye diagram, jitter, and connector/package discontinuities.
At high speed, the interconnect is part of the circuit, not a wire annotation.
Map load transient current, regulator bandwidth, decoupling hierarchy, plane impedance, and package inductance.
Capacitors are a distributed energy-delivery network; "more capacitance" in the wrong place may not help.
Where to go next in the module set
Pick by failure mode: circuit laws, reactive transients, filtering, amplification, systems/DSP, digital logic, embedded/VLSI, or SI/PI.
Module boundaries are pedagogical; real electronics failures often cross several layers.
